analysis.one_liner: Makes illegal robocalls and spoofed caller ID a jailable crime with stiffer fines.
analysis.headline: The bill won 40 bipartisan cosponsors but never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its subcommittee until Congress ended in January 2025. [S5]
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would give federal prosecutors a new criminal tool against illegal robocalls and texts. Someone who knowingly and willfully violates the ban on unwanted automated marketing calls could face up to a year in prison, and up to three years if they were repeat offenders, ran a massive calling operation, used the calls to further a felony, or cost victims $5,000 or more. It would also double the fine for knowingly faking caller ID information, from $10,000 to $20,000. [S2] [S3]
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone with a phone who gets illegal robocalls and scam texts. It targets the people running large calling operations and fraud schemes, the callers who spoof caller ID to trick people into answering, and repeat offenders. [S2] [S3]
analysis.who_benefits_short: Phone users hit by robocall scams

how_it_helps.text: Creates criminal penalties, including up to one year in prison, for anyone who willfully and knowingly violates the existing ban on unwanted automated marketing calls and texts.

Raises that to up to three years in prison for aggravated cases: repeat offenders, operations sending over 100,000 calls in a day or 10 million in a year, calls made to further a felony, or calls causing victims $5,000 or more in combined losses in a year.
Doubles the fine for knowingly transmitting misleading or inaccurate caller ID information from $10,000 to $20,000, hitting the spoofing tactics scammers use to disguise their calls.

analysis.who_pays: Operators of illegal robocall and robotext campaigns and caller-ID spoofers, who would face prison time and doubled fines. Legitimate telemarketers who follow the rules are unaffected, since the penalties apply only to willful and knowing violations. [S2] [S3]

drawbacks.text: The aggravated threshold of $5,000 in aggregate yearly losses is low enough that a mid-sized illegal calling operation could cross it routinely, and the definition of loss leaves room for dispute; prosecutors would have wide discretion over which violators face criminal charges rather than civil fines.

Congress has already banned these calls and set civil fines; the bill's new criminal penalties would only matter if actually prosecuted, and the bill includes no new funding or enforcement mandate for the agencies that would have to bring the cases.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a straightforward tightening of existing law. It adds real deterrent power — jail time for large-scale and repeat robocall violators and double fines for spoofing — at almost no cost to anyone except the people breaking the law. The main limits are that it creates no new enforcement resources and its low loss thresholds could sweep in smaller-scale violators, but neither weakness outweighs the benefit to the public it protects.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Communications and Technology Subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before the 118th Congress ended. [S5]

narrative.text: Representative David Kustoff introduced the bill on February 2, 2023, joined by Representative Deborah Ross. [S1]
The bill drew 40 cosponsors from both parties: 24 Republicans and 16 Democrats. [S4]
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on February 2, 2023, and to that committee's Subcommittee on Communications and Technology on February 10, 2023. [S5]
No further action was ever taken, and the bill died there when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Operators of illegal robocall campaigns and caller-ID spoofers, who continue to operate without facing the criminal penalties the bill would have created. Millions of phone users keep paying the cost in wasted time, scam losses, and unwanted calls. [S2] [S3] [S5]

sides.party_line_note: Support was clearly bipartisan: of the bill's 40 cosponsors, 24 were Republicans and 16 were Democrats. [S4]

industries.note: The bill's entire purpose is to criminalize their activity, adding up to three years in prison for large-scale or repeat operations and doubling spoofing fines. Their interest in blocking it runs directly against the public's interest in fewer scam calls. [S2] [S3]

Firms that knowingly violate telemarketing rules would face new criminal exposure under the bill, though companies following the rules are untouched since the penalties apply only to willful and knowing violations. [S3]
